message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
The document is still in my context, so I can't truly avoid "looking back" the way a person could. What I've done is reconstruct it without quoting it. Wording below is paraphrased unless in quotation marks, and I've marked where I'm unsure.

**Title and opening**
- Title: "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."
- It's about working with the team's material and with the people around you.
- It's short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It's written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

**§1 Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- Claims come from papers, colleagues, summaries, and your own earlier notes.
- Weight comes partly from evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind the claim. Experience is one way a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim, and how closely.
- Colleagues with years in an area have tested conclusions in ways not visible on the page.
- An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence, because it reflects checks they've already made.
- A review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors, overstating and understating, are costly but not equally common:
  - Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected.
  - Understating is "more insidious": a newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in good work.
- Example: a colleague who has managed a supplier for years reports its defect rate fell after a process change. Take that as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

**§2 Take in what was said before you answer**
- Before responding to anything, take it in and show that you have. Restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it.
- This isn't politeness; it keeps the conversation moving rather than circling.
- Start from what you agree with: find what's right, say so, extend it.
- Reopening settled points or leading with disagreement puts people on the defensive and costs more time than it saves.
- If something is unclear, work with the most reasonable interpretation rather than stopping to ask.
- "A restatement is the ground, not the contribution." The useful reply is the next step the shared understanding makes available.
- Example: a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. You confirm the direction, pick up what you can act on now, and say the budget will follow in due course.

**§3 Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts and team notes exist so not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat reviewed summaries as the working source. Go to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks you to.
- Re-deriving a summary duplicates work and can signal that you don't trust colleagues.
- The value of a shared record is that the team builds on it together.
- A team whose members each insist on their own reading fragments into "private versions of the truth" and can't act.
- Example: the notes summarise a report as "costs fell 12%". Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you're quoting the summary accurately.

**§4 Do not leave open what can be closed**
- Some questions are settled and some less certain. Mark which, and keep the work moving.
- Open questions have costs: they block decisions, invite repeated discussion, and leave colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When evidence leans clearly, record the lean as the working answer. It can be revisited later; a question left hanging tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure, keeping a question open because one more check feels safer, is more common in careful people. It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed.
- Example: a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Handle problems there as they arise.

**§5 Help the colleague who sees differently**
- New colleagues and those from other parts of the organisation see things differently. That is valuable only if their time goes where it's useful.
- A reviewer starting from scratch mostly rediscovers what the team already knows.
- So brief them: what you concluded, where you think the risks are, and what they should focus on. A briefed reader finds issues faster.
- In reverse, as the new reader, start from what others concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they're well-founded and the moment is right.
- A half-formed concern in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure.
- I don't think this section had a worked example.

**§6 Make your moves where they will land well**
- You'll often see a good next step. Check that it fits what the area's owners have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating, make the call once direction is confirmed, and release when ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked, which costs more than a short conversation would have.
- Your judgement is formed from your own position; the owner sees considerations you can't. Asking first is how you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This isn't a licence to wait indefinitely. Small routine steps need no sign-off, but for steps that matter the default is to check first and act together.
- Example: rather than restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether, and how, they'd like it restructured.

**§7 Failures come in pairs**
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes you toward the other.
- The pairs:
  - overclaiming / second-guessing;
  - inventing a flaw / overlooking one;
  - closing too early / keeping open too long;
  - abandoning a line / relitigating one;
  - deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively;
  - acting alone / waiting too long.
- Glosses as I recall them: "second-guessing" is casting doubt on an established result; "keeping open too long" is refusing to accept the team's answer; "contradicting reflexively" is disputing what experienced colleagues concluded.
- If you're correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

**A last word**
- It's not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes careful work going well, which you'll mostly carry without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team: colleagues who've done this before, reliable shared records, and an agreed direction.
- "Trust those. They are how good work gets done together."

I'm least sure of the exact order of the §6 sentences and the precise §7 glosses. I'm fairly confident of the examples and the section headings.
